## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, government, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. For a legal or regulatory question, firecrawl_gov_search searches primary law and regulatory material from US federal, state, and local government sources: statutes, regulations, codes, court opinions, and other government publications; firecrawl_search with categories: ["gov"] reaches the same sources in the web group and cannot be combined with other categories. For a biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature question, the firecrawl_research_* tools search the paper index, while categories: ["research"] on firecrawl_search filters ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites. Use the firecrawl_research_* tools to search academic and research literature, expand from anchor papers via the citation graph, and read full-text passages from a specific paper. Search and discovery tools are read-only and return ranked results. Billing: web, developer, and research search are billed per request; government search is free; Alexandria discovery (firecrawl_search with sources ["alexandria"] alone, and firecrawl_find_tools) is free; firecrawl_scrape is billed, as a page retrieval in url mode or at each executed capability's listed price in alexandria mode.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects, scoped to the
caller's HeyGen account via OAuth bearer token.

## Available Tools

### Feedback
- **submit_feedback** — Submit feedback the user expressed, or a meaningful terminal
  HyperFrames failure observed after supported recovery failed. Use `source="user"` only
  for the user's statement and `source="agent"` for an agent observation. Submit once per
  issue; omit secrets, raw media, and unrelated conversation text. Expected "project still
  building" responses and redirects to local HyperFrames skills are normal product behavior,
  so they are not automatically reported as failures.

### Author / Edit
- **compose** — Author a new HyperFrames project or apply an edit to an existing
  one. Pass `project_id` from a previous tool call to continue editing the same
  project; leave it empty (or omit) to start a new one. Returns immediately while
  the agent runs in the background (typically a few minutes). An optional
  `design_source` argument picks the brand style: a new project defaults to one of the
  vetted looks (`claude`, `blockframe`, or `monochrome`), with `mat` and `signal` also
  available as built-in presets. The compose response names the style that was applied and
  lists the alternatives, so a first video — when the user hasn't expressed a style
  preference — is a natural moment to let them know a different look is one follow-up
  away. On a follow-up edit, leaving `design_source` out keeps the project's current
  style; it's passed on an edit only to deliberately reskin.

### Read
- **list_projects** — List the caller's projects, newest first. Cursor-paginated

57	    ABSTRACT                                                                                                                        ARTICLE HISTORY
58	    Objectives: The purpose of this study was to analyse the association of the workload monotony and workload                      Accepted 25 July 2018
59	    strain with the injury incidence with professional football players taking part in European football competitions.
60	                                                                                                                                    KEYWORDS
61	    Methods: A total of 130 elite football players, from 5 teams playing European competitions, have been
62	                                                                                                                                    Team sport; training; injury
63	    followed during a season. The internal workload was calculated using the Session Rate of Perceived                              prevention
64	    Exertion method and the injuries were recorded. The 4-weeks, 3-weeks, 2-weeks and 1-week monotony
65	    (mean workload divided by workload standard deviation) and strain (absolute workload multiplied by
66	    monotony) were calculated on a daily basis, using a rolling days method.
67	    Results: The 4-weeks monotony was related to injury incidence. The relative risk (RR) of injury is
68	    decreased with an increase in 4-weeks monotony (RR = 0.72, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.58–0.90;
69	    P = 0.004). The injury incidence was related to the 4-weeks strain. The RR of injury is increased with an
70	    increase 4-weeks strain (RR = 1.50, 95% CI 1.14–1.97; P = 0.004).
71	    Conclusions: The links between a high 4-weeks monotony and the injury incidence, and the links
72	    between a high 4-weeks strain and the injury incidence indicate that monotony and strain were
73	    associated with injury incidence in elite football players and require to be monitored.

    ABSTRACT                                                                                                                        ARTICLE HISTORY
    Objectives: The purpose of this study was to analyse the association of the workload monotony and workload                      Accepted 25 July 2018
    strain with the injury incidence with professional football players taking part in European football competitions.
                                                                                                                                    KEYWORDS
    Methods: A total of 130 elite football players, from 5 teams playing European competitions, have been
                                                                                                                                    Team sport; training; injury
    followed during a season. The internal workload was calculated using the Session Rate of Perceived                              prevention
    Exertion method and the injuries were recorded. The 4-weeks, 3-weeks, 2-weeks and 1-week monotony
    (mean workload divided by workload standard deviation) and strain (absolute workload multiplied by
    monotony) were calculated on a daily basis, using a rolling days method.
    Results: The 4-weeks monotony was related to injury incidence. The relative risk (RR) of injury is
    decreased with an increase in 4-weeks monotony (RR = 0.72, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.58–0.90;
    P = 0.004). The injury incidence was related to the 4-weeks strain. The RR of injury is increased with an
    increase 4-weeks strain (RR = 1.50, 95% CI 1.14–1.97; P = 0.004).
    Conclusions: The links between a high 4-weeks monotony and the injury incidence, and the links
    between a high 4-weeks strain and the injury incidence indicate that monotony and strain were
    associated with injury incidence in elite football players and require to be monitored.

76	Abstract
77	The current study introduces a new index for external and internal workload, “workload efficiency”, and assesses in
78	professional soccer the influence of pre-match training load on match workload efficiency. External and internal
79	workloads were determined for 44 training sessions and 16 competitive matches using a 10-Hz global positioning system
80	(GPS) and a 200 Hz accelerometer/heart rate monitor. Training loads were registered from day five (D-5) to day one (D-
81	1) prior to each competitive match. Workload efficiency was calculated for each match as the ratio between overall
82	external and internal load. A multiple stepwise regression analysis (including z-transformed variables) was used to
83	determine training load variables that predict workload efficiency of the following matches. Training load variables of the
84	previous days explained 26.6% of the variance in workload efficiency during the following matches. Long sprinting
85	distance on D-3 and D-4 and total distance on D-1 positively influenced the players’ workload efficiency, whereas long
86	training durations and high training load on D-1 showed adverse effects. The present outcomes suggest that including
87	sprint training (high sprinting distance) four and three days prior to a match, may provide a positive stimulus for the
88	subsequent workload efficiency in matches. The negative impact of long training duration and high training load one day
89	before the game highlights the importance of a diligent planning of the immediate competition preparation phase. This
90	study shows that workload efficiency is a useful metric to assess match performance and that body-worn sensor technology
91	can be useful for tailoring training loads.
92	
93	KEYWORDS: Football, athlete performance, internal and external load, wearable technology, global positioning system
94	GPS, motion tracking systems
95	
96	Highlights
97	. Wearable sensor technology that combines motion tracking technology with heart rate monitors may provide detailed
98	  information on the external and internal workload in soccer.
99	. The current study introduces a new index, named workload efficiency, based on earlier concepts of internal and external
100	  workload ratios.
101	. The study combines internal (TRIMPMOD) and external (equivalent distance) workload parameters that specifically
102	  focus on intermittent sports.
103	. As a proof of concept the current study investigated whether weekly training load of a professional soccer team was related
104	  to the newly introduced index during the following matches.

Workload efficiency as a new tool to describe external and internal
competitive match load of a professional soccer team: A descriptive
study on the relationship between pre-game training loads and relative
match load


JOHANNES GRÜNBICHLER1, PETER FEDEROLF                                         1
                                                                                  , & HANNES GATTERER                     12


1
 Department of Sport Science, University of Innsbruck, Innsbruck, Austria & 2Institute of Mountain Emergency Medicine,
Eurac Research, Bolzano, Italy



Abstract
The current study introduces a new index for external and internal workload, “workload efficiency”, and assesses in
professional soccer the influence of pre-match training load on match workload efficiency. External and internal
workloads were determined for 44 training sessions and 16 competitive matches using a 10-Hz global positioning system
(GPS) and a 200 Hz accelerometer/heart rate monitor. Training loads were registered from day five (D-5) to day one (D-
1) prior to each competitive match. Workload efficiency was calculated for each match as the ratio between overall
external and internal load. A multiple stepwise regression analysis (including z-transformed variables) was used to
determine training load variables that predict workload efficiency of the following matches. Training load variables of the
previous days explained 26.6% of the variance in workload efficiency during the following matches. Long sprinting
distance on D-3 and D-4 and total distance on D-1 positively influenced the players’ workload efficiency, whereas long
training durations and high training load on D-1 showed adverse effects. The present outcomes suggest that including
sprint training (high sprinting distance) four and three days prior to a match, may provide a positive stimulus for the
subsequent workload efficiency in matches. The negative impact of long training duration and high training load one day
before the game highlights the importance of a diligent planning of the immediate competition preparation phase. This
study shows that workload efficiency is a useful metric to assess match performance and that body-worn sensor technology
can be useful for tailoring training loads.

KEYWORDS: Football, athlete performance, internal and external load, wearable technology, global positioning system
GPS, motion tracking systems

Highlights
. Wearable sensor technology that combines motion tracking technology with heart rate monitors may provide detailed
  information on the external and internal workload in soccer.
. The current study introduces a new index, named workload efficiency, based on earlier concepts of internal and external
  workload ratios.
. The study combines internal (TRIMPMOD) and external (equivalent distance) workload parameters that specifically
  focus on intermittent sports.
. As a proof of concept the current study investigated whether weekly training load of a professional soccer team was related
  to the newly introduced index during the following matches.

51	Accepted: 18 January 2023                      In competitive sports, pursuing optimal athletic performance is the ultimate goal
52	Published: 22 January 2023                for athletes [1]. During past decades, sport psychologists have developed diverse psy-
53	                                          chological training approaches, endeavoring to help athletes promote their competitive
54	                                          performance [2]. As a traditional stream of psychological training, cognitive behavioral
55	                                          therapies (CBTs) have been widely applied and shown effectiveness in the promotion
56	Copyright: © 2023 by the authors.
57	                                          of athletic performance among athletes [3]. CBT emphasizes the self-control of internal

59	                                          states through the training of psychological skills, with a view of improving motor perfor-

75	 Int. J. Environ. Res. Public Health 2023, 20, 2038                                                                               2 of 16
76	
77	
78	
79	
80	                                              To address the limitations of traditional CBTs, mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs)
81	                                        have raised increasing concerns, which have shown a great potential for promoting ath-
82	                                        letes’ competitive performances as an alternative of traditional psychological training
83	                                        approaches [6]. The term of mindfulness is derived from Eastern Zen [7], which is defined
84	                                        as non-judgmental, conscious, purposeful focus, understanding, and acceptance of the
85	                                        things around one in the present moment [8]. In contrast to the traditional behavioral
86	                                        therapies, mindfulness emphasized that individuals should be aware of and experience
87	                                        the internal and external thoughts and feelings without any judgments [9]. In the sports
88	                                        domain, mindfulness has been used to cultivate athletes’ abilities to accept and realize, to
89	                                        inspire athletes to effectively control their attention and improve their body perception
90	                                        ability [8–10]. Mindfulness underlines the process from perceiving to experiencing the
91	                                        constant changes of current things and one’s own emotions without the inhibition and
92	                                        control of undesirable responses in order to remove the emotional state of pervious worries,
93	                                        avoid performance failure under pressure, and adjust the mental state of athletes [11].
94	                                        Mindfulness provides a potential not only to improve performance but also to decrease the
95	                                        risks of mental health problems [11].
96	                                              With increasing understandings of the mechanisms of mindfulness with different
97	                                        outcomes, a series of mindfulness training approaches have been developed, such as
98	                                        Mindfulness-Acceptance-Commitment (MAC) training, Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduc-
99	                                        tion (MBSR) training, and Mindfulness-based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT) [12–15]. Mind-
100	                                        fulness has shown to be positively associated with a wide range of indicators among
101	                                        athletes, including greater athletic performance, better mindfulness, and related psycho-
102	                                        logical components (e.g., acceptance, flow, and psychological flexibility) and lower risks
103	                                        of mental health problems (e.g., stress, anxiety, depression, and burnout) [9,11–15]. Two
104	                                        previous review and meta-analysis studies compiling evidence from diverse types of
105	                                        studies (e.g., RCT, case study, and observational) provided preliminary support for the
106	                                        effectiveness of mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) on improving athletes’ sports
107	                                        performance [9,12,16]. Furthermore, previous review papers have also examined the ef-
108	                                        fects of MBIs on the mindfulness-related psychological components (i.e., flow) and mental
109	                                        health among specific athlete samples (e.g., elite athletes and long-distance runners) [17–19].
110	                                        However, none of previous review studies focused only on the evidence from RCTs (the
111	                                        rigorous study design), which may be due to the limited numbers of studies. In addition,
112	                                        the above review studies did not provide a comprehensive overview of the effectiveness
113	                                        of MBIs on a wide range of outcomes (i.e., performance, psychological components, and
114	                                        mental health) targeting all types of athletes (e.g., elite, collegiate, and retired).
115	                                              Therefore, the present study aimed to systemically review and meta-analyze existing
116	                                        RCT evidence on the effects of MBIs in improving athletic performance, mindfulness, and
117	                                        mindfulness-related psychological components and mental health among athletes. It is ex-
118	                                        pected that the research findings may contribute to future mindfulness research, interventions,
119	                                        and policymaking, with the aim of promoting sport performance and health among athletes.
120	
121	                                        2. Materials and Methods
122	                                        2.1. Search Strategy and Study Selection
123	                                              The current systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted following the Pre-
124	                                        ferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines
125	                                        (Supplementary Materials); the review protocol has been prospectively registered on PROS-
126	                                        PERO (CRD42022299940). Based on a predefined literature search strategy, the following
127	                                        five electronic databases were searched using Boolean logic’s multi-filed search format with
128	                                        no limit to the date range: Web of Science, PubMed, Scopus, ProQuest, and ScienceDirect.
129	                                        In addition, the reference lists of relevant review papers were also checked. We combined
130	                                        three groups of keywords in the search: (1) mindfulness; (2) sport* OR athlete* OR player* OR
131	                                        athletic* OR exercise* OR training; and (3) performance OR achievement. The literature search
132	                                        was limited to human participants and the publication language was limited to English.
133	 Int. J. Environ. Res. Public Health 2023, 20, 2038                                                                                  3 of 16
134	
135	
136	
137	
138	                                              Following the Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, and Study design
139	                                        (PICOS) principles, the study selection criteria included:
140	                                              Population: any types of athletes without limits to the demographics and sports levels (e.g.,
141	                                        collegiate, recreational/amateur, professional, elite, retired, or handicapped) were included.
142	                                              Intervention: any types of mindfulness-based interventions (MBI) without limits to the
143	                                        training types and components (e.g., traditional Mindfulness-Acceptance-Commitment
144	                                        intervention, Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction intervention, mindfulness-based yoga,
145	                                        or mindfulness-based cognitive therapy), frequency, and duration were included.
146	                                              Comparison: any control conditions without mindfulness components (e.g., non-
147	                                        treatment control, waiting-list control, and active control using CBT) were eligible.
148	                                              Outcome: objectively or subjectively measured athletic performance was the primary
149	                                        outcome and secondary outcomes included the mindfulness level, mindfulness-related psy-
150	                                        chological components (e.g., acceptance, self-compassion, psychological flexibility, flow, and
151	                                        ruminative response) and mental health indicators (e.g., anxiety, stress, and depression).
152	                                              Study design: due to the large number of studies found in the literature search after
153	                                        protocol submission, we decided to limit our analysis to randomized controlled trials
154	                                        (RCTs) as this type of study provided the highest standard of evidence. All the RCT designs
155	                                        were included, while quasi-experimental, observational, and case studies were excluded.
156	                                              In addition, book chapters, editorial letters, commentaries, conference proceedings,
157	                                        qualitative articles, and review articles were not eligible for inclusion.
158	                                              All the initially searched articles were exported into the Mendeley to remove the dupli-
159	                                        cations. Two investigators (W.Y. and F.J.J.) independently screened the titles and abstracts
160	                                        of all the remaining articles, where all clearly irrelevant articles were deleted. Afterwards,
161	                                        the full texts of all the identified articles were checked for eligibility by two investigators
162	                                        independently according to the aforementioned inclusion criteria. During the review process,
163	                                        any disagreements were addressed by consensus or by involving a third investigator (SML).
164	
165	                                        2.2. Data Extraction
166	                                             A standardized form was used to extract data from the full texts of eligible articles by
167	                                        one investigator (WY). A second investigator (FJJ) checked the accuracy of the data extrac-
168	                                        tion. All the information including authors, publication year, study design, participants,
169	                                        sample size, mean age, intervention duration, frequency, measures, and main findings were
170	                                        extracted to the Excel sheet for the following narrative synthesis and meta-analysis.
171	
172	                                        2.3. Risk of Bias Assessment
173	                                              The study quality of included studies was evaluated using the Cochrane risk-of-
174	                                        bias tool in Review Manager software (RevMan, version 5.4, Cochrane Collaboration,
175	                                        Oxford, UK). Seven aspects of biases, including random sequence generation (selection
176	                                        bias), concealment of allocation sequence (selection bias), blinding of participants and
177	                                        personnel (performance bias), blinding of outcome assessment (detection bias), incomplete
178	                                        outcome data (attrition bias), selective outcome reporting (reporting bias), and others,
179	                                        were assessed. The overall quality of the study was categorized as low risk (“low risk”
180	                                        in all aspects), unclear risk (at least one aspect with “some concerns of biases”), and high
181	                                        risk (at least one aspect with “high risk” or several aspects with “some concerns”). The
182	                                        study quality was evaluated by two investigators (W.Y. and F.J.J.) independently and any
183	                                        discrepancies were resolved by consensus or confirmation of a third investigator (SML).
184	
185	                                        2.4. Statistical Analysis
186	                                             The meta-analyses were implemented using RevMan 5.4 (Cochrane Collaboration,
187	                                        Oxford, UK) if at least three studies presented the same exposure with adequate information
188	                                        for the effect size estimates [20–22]. The standardized mean difference (SMD) with 95%
189	                                        confidence intervals (CI) was extracted from the pre- and post-intervention. For studies
190	                                        that reported other effect sizes (e.g., odds ratio and Cohen’s f 2 ), the SMDs were calculated
191	                                        using a conversion spreadsheet [22,23]. Pooled effect sizes were estimated using a random
192	 Int. J. Environ. Res. Public Health 2023, 20, 2038                                                                                             4 of 16
193	
194	
195	
196	
197	                                        effects model and were presented in forest plots. The heterogeneity was assessed using the
198	                                        I2 , with I2 values of 25%, 50%, and 75% indicating low, medium, and high heterogeneity,
199	                                        respectively [24]. The publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots and Egger’s
200	                                        regression tests [25,26]. The subgroup analyses were implemented on study quality and
201	                                        demographics in case the number of included samples is no less than 10 [22,27,28]. The
202	                                        statistical significance level was set as p < 0.05 for effect sizes estimation and p < 0.10 for
203	                                        heterogeneity and publication bias assessments [27,28].
204	
205	                                        3. Results
206	                                        3.1. Study Characteristics
207	                                                        Figure 1 shows the PRISMA flow diagram. Initially, we retrieved 3072 records from
208	                                               the databases search and identified an additional five articles from other sources. After the
209	                                               duplicates were removed, 1897 articles were screened by two investigators at the title and
210	                                               abstract

Effects of Mindfulness-Based Interventions on Promoting
Athletic Performance and Related Factors among Athletes:
A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized

Yan Wang 1 , Si-Man Lei 1, *              and Jingjing Fan 2

                                          Abstract: In recent years, mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) have been widely applied in
                                          competition sports with respect to athletic performance and mental health promotion, whereas
                                          evidence of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) has not been well summarized. Therefore, this study
                                          aimed to systematically review and meta-analyze the existing evidence on the effects of MBIs on
                                          improving athletic performance, mindfulness level, mindfulness-related psychological components
                                          (e.g., acceptance, self-compassion, flow), and mental health (e.g., burnout, stress, psychological well-
                                          being) among athletes. Following the PRISMA guidelines, a literature search was implemented on
                                          five electronic databases (Web of Science, PubMed, Scopus, ProQuest, and ScienceDirect) and relevant
                                          review papers. The article selection, risk of bias assessment, and data extraction were performed
                                          by two investigators independently. The standardized mean difference (SMD) was calculated to
                                          evaluate the effects of interventions using the random effect model. Among the 1897 original hits,
                                          thirty-two eligible RCT studies were included in the systematic review, of which seven were involved
                                          in the meta-analysis. The results showed that MBIs were effective in promoting athletes’ athletic

 Int. J. Environ. Res. Public Health 2023, 20, 2038                                                                               2 of 16




                                              To address the limitations of traditional CBTs, mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs)
                                        have raised increasing concerns, which have shown a great potential for promoting ath-
                                        letes’ competitive performances as an alternative of traditional psychological training
                                        approaches [6]. The term of mindfulness is derived from Eastern Zen [7], which is defined
                                        as non-judgmental, conscious, purposeful focus, understanding, and acceptance of the
                                        things around one in the present moment [8]. In contrast to the traditional behavioral
                                        therapies, mindfulness emphasized that individuals should be aware of and experience
                                        the internal and external thoughts and feelings without any judgments [9]. In the sports
                                        domain, mindfulness has been used to cultivate athletes’ abilities to accept and realize, to
                                        inspire athletes to effectively control their attention and improve their body perception
                                        ability [8–10]. Mindfulness underlines the process from perceiving to experiencing the
                                        constant changes of current things and one’s own emotions without the inhibition and
                                        control of undesirable responses in order to remove the emotional state of pervious worries,
                                        avoid performance failure under pressure, and adjust the mental state of athletes [11].
                                        Mindfulness provides a potential not only to improve performance but also to decrease the
                                        risks of mental health problems [11].
                                              With increasing understandings of the mechanisms of mindfulness with different
                                        outcomes, a series of mindfulness training approaches have been developed, such as
                                        Mindfulness-Acceptance-Commitment (MAC) training, Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduc-
                                        tion (MBSR) training, and Mindfulness-based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT) [12–15]. Mind-
                                        fulness has shown to be positively associated with a wide range of indicators among
                                        athletes, including greater athletic performance, better mindfulness, and related psycho-
                                        logical components (e.g., acceptance, flow, and psychological flexibility) and lower risks
                                        of mental health problems (e.g., stress, anxiety, depression, and burnout) [9,11–15]. Two
                                        previous review and meta-analysis studies compiling evidence from diverse types of
                                        studies (e.g., RCT, case study, and observational) provided preliminary support for the
                                        effectiveness of mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) on improving athletes’ sports
                                        performance [9,12,16]. Furthermore, previous review papers have also examined the ef-
                                        fects of MBIs on the mindfulness-related psychological components (i.e., flow) and mental
                                        health among specific athlete samples (e.g., elite athletes and long-distance runners) [17–19].
                                        However, none of previous review studies focused only on the evidence from RCTs (the
                                        rigorous study design), which may be due to the limited numbers of studies. In addition,
                                        the above review studies did not provide a comprehensive overview of the effectiveness
                                        of MBIs on a wide range of outcomes (i.e., performance, psychological components, and
                                        mental health) targeting all types of athletes (e.g., elite, collegiate, and retired).
                                              Therefore, the present study aimed to systemically review and meta-analyze existing
                                        RCT evidence on the effects of MBIs in improving athletic performance, mindfulness, and
                                        mindfulness-related psychological components and mental health among athletes. It is ex-
                                        pected that the research findings may contribute to future mindfulness research, interventions,
                                        and policymaking, with the aim of promoting sport performance and health among athletes.

                                        2. Materials and Methods
                                        2.1. Search Strategy and Study Selection
                                              The current systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted following the Pre-
                                        ferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines
                                        (Supplementary Materials); the review protocol has been prospectively registered on PROS-
                                        PERO (CRD42022299940). Based on a predefined literature search strategy, the following
                                        five electronic databases were searched using Boolean logic’s multi-filed search format with
                                        no limit to the date range: Web of Science, PubMed, Scopus, ProQuest, and ScienceDirect.
                                        In addition, the reference lists of relevant review papers were also checked. We combined
                                        three groups of keywords in the search: (1) mindfulness; (2) sport* OR athlete* OR player* OR
                                        athletic* OR exercise* OR training; and (3) performance OR achievement. The literature search
                                        was limited to human participants and the publication language was limited to English.
 Int. J. Environ. Res. Public Health 2023, 20, 2038                                                                                  3 of 16




                                              Following the Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, and Study design
                                        (PICOS) principles, the study selection criteria included:
                                              Population: any types of athletes without limits to the demographics and sports levels (e.g.,
                                        collegiate, recreational/amateur, professional, elite, retired, or handicapped) were included.
                                              Intervention: any types of mindfulness-based interventions (MBI) without limits to the
                                        training types and components (e.g., traditional Mindfulness-Acceptance-Commitment
                                        intervention, Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction intervention, mindfulness-based yoga,
                                        or mindfulness-based cognitive therapy), frequency, and duration were included.
                                              Comparison: any control conditions without mindfulness components (e.g., non-
                                        treatment control, waiting-list control, and active control using CBT) were eligible.
                                              Outcome: objectively or subjectively measured athletic performance was the primary
                                        outcome and secondary outcomes included the mindfulness level, mindfulness-related psy-
                                        chological components (e.g., acceptance, self-compassion, psychological flexibility, flow, and
                                        ruminative response) and mental health indicators (e.g., anxiety, stress, and depression).
                                              Study design: due to the large number of studies found in the literature search after
                                        protocol submission, we decided to limit our analysis to randomized controlled trials
                                        (RCTs) as this type of study provided the highest standard of evidence. All the RCT designs
                                        were included, while quasi-experimental, observational, and case studies were excluded.
                                              In addition, book chapters, editorial letters, commentaries, conference proceedings,
                                        qualitative articles, and review articles were not eligible for inclusion.
                                              All the initially searched articles were exported into the Mendeley to remove the dupli-
                                        cations. Two investigators (W.Y. and F.J.J.) independently screened the titles and abstracts
                                        of all the remaining articles, where all clearly irrelevant articles were deleted. Afterwards,
                                        the full texts of all the identified articles were checked for eligibility by two investigators
                                        independently according to the aforementioned inclusion criteria. During the review process,
                                        any disagreements were addressed by consensus or by involving a third investigator (SML).

                                        2.2. Data Extraction
                                             A standardized form was used to extract data from the full texts of eligible articles by
                                        one investigator (WY). A second investigator (FJJ) checked the accuracy of the data extrac-
                                        tion. All the information including authors, publication year, study design, participants,
                                        sample size, mean age, intervention duration, frequency, measures, and main findings were
                                        extracted to the Excel sheet for the following narrative synthesis and meta-analysis.

                                        2.3. Risk of Bias Assessment
                                              The study quality of included studies was evaluated using the Cochrane risk-of-
                                        bias tool in Review Manager software (RevMan, version 5.4, Cochrane Collaboration,
                                        Oxford, UK). Seven aspects of biases, including random sequence generation (selection
                                        bias), concealment of allocation sequence (selection bias), blinding of participants and
                                        personnel (performance bias), blinding of outcome assessment (detection bias), incomplete
                                        outcome data (attrition bias), selective outcome reporting (reporting bias), and others,
                                        were assessed. The overall quality of the study was categorized as low risk (“low risk”
                                        in all aspects), unclear risk (at least one aspect with “some concerns of biases”), and high
                                        risk (at least one aspect with “high risk” or several aspects with “some concerns”). The
                                        study quality was evaluated by two investigators (W.Y. and F.J.J.) independently and any
                                        discrepancies were resolved by consensus or confirmation of a third investigator (SML).

                                        2.4. Statistical Analysis
                                             The meta-analyses were implemented using RevMan 5.4 (Cochrane Collaboration,
                                        Oxford, UK) if at least three studies presented the same exposure with adequate information
                                        for the effect size estimates [20–22]. The standardized mean difference (SMD) with 95%
                                        confidence intervals (CI) was extracted from the pre- and post-intervention. For studies
                                        that reported other effect sizes (e.g., odds ratio and Cohen’s f 2 ), the SMDs were calculated
                                        using a conversion spreadsheet [22,23]. Pooled effect sizes were estimated using a random
 Int. J. Environ. Res. Public Health 2023, 20, 2038                                                                                             4 of 16




                                        effects model and were presented in forest plots. The heterogeneity was assessed using the
                                        I2 , with I2 values of 25%, 50%, and 75% indicating low, medium, and high heterogeneity,
                                        respectively [24]. The publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots and Egger’s
                                        regression tests [25,26]. The subgroup analyses were implemented on study quality and
                                        demographics in case the number of included samples is no less than 10 [22,27,28]. The
                                        statistical significance level was set as p < 0.05 for effect sizes estimation and p < 0.10 for
                                        heterogeneity and publication bias assessments [27,28].

570	                                              Consistent results were observed in the included studies, showing significant improve-
571	                                        ments in sport performance following MBIs. Specifically, a randomized controlled trial [29]
572	                                        examined the effects of a 15 min mindfulness intervention on basketball players’ athletic
573	                                        performance under pressure. The results showed that 15 min mindfulness intervention was
574	                                        effective in promoting participants’ first free-throw performance under a stressful setting
575	                                        compared to the control condition. In another study [30], the results found that partici-
576	                                        pants in the intervention group (n = 18) receiving a 15 min mindfulness treatment had a
577	                                        small-to-moderate increase (Cohen’s d = 0.48) in free-throw performance compared with
578	                                        the control group (n = 18). Another RCT study [31] which examined the effectiveness of
579	                                        an eight-session MAC method on improving performance and sports competition anxiety
580	                                        in athletes found that MAC was effective in improving athletic performance compared to
581	                                        the control group. An American research group investigated the effectiveness of the MAC
582	                                        approach compared to traditional psychological skills training (PST) for mental health and
583	                                        sport performance [13]. The results indicated that the MAC group outperformed the PST
584	                                        group on the outcomes. There was also a significant within-group effect, where the MAC
585	                                        participants experienced significant increases in sport performance from pre-intervention
586	                                        to post-intervention (p = 0.04). In another study [32], compared with the PST group (n = 33),
587	                                        the MAC group (n = 36) reported higher levels of training performance (β = −0.10, 95%
588	                                        CI = [−0.14, −0.08] among elite athletes. In addition, a pilot study of MBSoccerP [39]
589	                                        explored the potential role of mindfulness and other psychological factors on flow and elite
590	                                        performance in soccer athletes. The results showed that after receiving eight 1.5–2 h weekly
591	                                        sessions of MBSoccerP, mindfulness mediated the peak performance of elite soccer players.
592	                                        In a Swiss study [33], researchers tested elite athletes (n = 133) from twenty-three different
593	                                        sports and the results indicated that the trait mindfulness was related to fewer performance

603	                                        performance enhancement (MSPE) intervention (90 min each week) significantly increased
604	                                        the self-rated sport performance compared to the control condition [36]. In a Portuguese
605	                                        study of twenty-eight elite soccer athletes [38], the results indicated that MBSoccerP was
606	                                        effective in enhancing elite soccer athletes’ performance compared to the control group. In

608	                                        and found that ACT had significant effects on both objective performance outcomes (goals,

611	                                        after the MBI, the participants reported greater sport enjoyment, less negative internal

                                        3.2. Effects of Mindfulness-Based Interventions on Athletic Performance among Athletes
                                              Consistent results were observed in the included studies, showing significant improve-
                                        ments in sport performance following MBIs. Specifically, a randomized controlled trial [29]
                                        examined the effects of a 15 min mindfulness intervention on basketball players’ athletic
                                        performance under pressure. The results showed that 15 min mindfulness intervention was
                                        effective in promoting participants’ first free-throw performance under a stressful setting
                                        compared to the control condition. In another study [30], the results found that partici-
                                        pants in the intervention group (n = 18) receiving a 15 min mindfulness treatment had a
                                        small-to-moderate increase (Cohen’s d = 0.48) in free-throw performance compared with
                                        the control group (n = 18). Another RCT study [31] which examined the effectiveness of
                                        an eight-session MAC method on improving performance and sports competition anxiety
                                        in athletes found that MAC was effective in improving athletic performance compared to
                                        the control group. An American research group investigated the effectiveness of the MAC
                                        approach compared to traditional psychological skills training (PST) for mental health and
                                        sport performance [13]. The results indicated that the MAC group outperformed the PST
                                        group on the outcomes. There was also a significant within-group effect, where the MAC
                                        participants experienced significant increases in sport performance from pre-intervention
                                        to post-intervention (p = 0.04). In another study [32], compared with the PST group (n = 33),
                                        the MAC group (n = 36) reported higher levels of training performance (β = −0.10, 95%
                                        CI = [−0.14, −0.08] among elite athletes. In addition, a pilot study of MBSoccerP [39]
                                        explored the potential role of mindfulness and other psychological factors on flow and elite
                                        performance in soccer athletes. The results showed that after receiving eight 1.5–2 h weekly
                                        sessions of MBSoccerP, mindfulness mediated the peak performance of elite soccer players.
                                        In a Swiss study [33], researchers tested elite athletes (n = 133) from twenty-three different
                                        sports and the results indicated that the trait mindfulness was related to fewer performance
                                        worries and prevented the remaining worries from influencing athletes’ behavior, thereby
                                        helping them to perform better. As for the two studies of MMT, one of them estimated the
                                        effect of MMT on shooting performance in elite shooters (n = 96) and was assessed using a
                                        pre-and-post-test approach [34]. Compared to the control, the results of the experimental
                                        group showed that MMT intervention decreased pre-competition stress and enhanced
                                        shooting performance. Another one also examined the effect of MMT on 110 shooters [35].
                                        The duration of intervention lasted for 4 weeks and the results indicated that MMT en-
                                        hanced sports performance (p < 0.001) compared to the control group. In another study
                                        of fifty-two university athletes, the participants who received a six-week mindful sport
                                        performance enhancement (MSPE) intervention (90 min each week) significantly increased
                                        the self-rated sport performance compared to the control condition [36]. In a Portuguese
                                        study of twenty-eight elite soccer athletes [38], the results indicated that MBSoccerP was
                                        effective in enhancing elite soccer athletes’ performance compared to the control group. In
                                        addition, one study used the ACT method to intervene on 34 junior elite ice hockey players
                                        and found that ACT had significant effects on both objective performance outcomes (goals,
                                        assists, and taken shots) and blinded coach ratings of players performance in comparison
                                        with the control condition [57]. Another study with 24 collegiate students found that
                                        after the MBI, the participants reported greater sport enjoyment, less negative internal
                                        states of current sport performance, and greater improvements in satisfaction with sport
                                        performance compared to the PST group [58].

                                        letes [48]. A Switzerland research group investigated the effectiveness of the MI approach

                                        in athletes [33]. Elite athletes from 23 different sports were selected (n = 133) and the

1322	                                        4. Discussion
1323	                                              This is the first study that systematically reviewed and meta-analyzed the RCT ev-
1324	                                        idence regarding the effectiveness of MBIs on athletic performance, mindfulness levels,
1325	                                        mindfulness-related psychological components, and mental health outcomes among ath-
1326	                                        letes. Thirty-two eligible studies were included in the narrative synthesis, of which nineteen
1327	                                        were included in the quantitative analysis. Narratively, the MBIs were effective in promot-
1328	                                        ing athletes’ sports performance. The results of the meta-analysis found that MBIs showed
1329	                                        effectiveness on improving the mindfulness and mindfulness-based psychological compo-
1330	                                        nents, yet no significant effects were found for mental health outcomes among athletes.
1331	                                              For athletic performance, from the narrative synthesis, we found that all the included
1332	                                        studies indicated a significant improvement in the performance indicators after receiving
1333	                                        the MBI. Our finding is consistent with the previous review papers supporting for the
1334	                                        effectiveness of MBIs on athletes’ sport performance [9,12]. However, due to the limited
1335	                                        evidence and considerable variety in the outcome measures, a quantitative synthesis is
1336	                                        not available. More studies using an RCT design to examine the effects of using MBIs in
1337	                                        athletes’ sports performance are needed in the future.
1338	                                              For mindfulness levels, in accordance with previous evidence [59,60], our study found
1339	                                        that MBIs could significantly improve the athletes’ mindfulness levels. For the mindfulness-
1340	                                        related psychological components (e.g., acceptance, flow, psychological flexibility, and
1341	                                        ruminative response), we found a significant effect of MBIs on improving these indicators,
1342	                                        which is in line with previous evidence among different types of athletes and general
1343	                                        populations [10,61,62]. During the games, it is easy for athletes to experience negative
1344	                                        emotions, such as nervousness and worries [63,64]. On game day, players may experience
1345	                                        dissatisfaction with their performance, negative thinking, reality avoidance, and immersion
1346	                                        in unpleasant emotions due to off-court circumstances, such as the unfavorable response
1347	                                        of the crowd or losing points [65,66]. Mindfulness may play a crucial role in addressing
1348	                                        these problems for athletes. Our research findings preliminarily supported the effects of
1349	                                        MBIs on improving these mindfulness-related psychological components, implying that,
1350	                                        in future practice, MBI could be applied in relevant sports domains to achieve specific
1351	                                        training targets (e.g., enhancement of emotion control, prevention of performance failure
1352	                                        under pressure, and improvement of flow and commitment).
1353	                                              For the mental health outcomes, our findings were inconsistent with the previous evi-
1354	                                        dence that showed that MBIs were effective in improving mental health symptoms [19,62].
1355	                                        The potential reasons for the discrepancy may be multifaceted. For example, our review
1356	                                        targeted all types of athletes, while previous studies focused on the elite athletes or general
1357	                                        populations. Another reason MBIs may have not demonstrated improvements in mental
1358	                                        health symptoms of athletes is because the athletes in the studies that were selected for
1359	                                        our review are not clinical populations. It may have been that athletes’ mental health
1360	                                        symptoms were already low; therefore, changes in mental health outcomes may have been
1361	                                        inconsequential. In addition, we only included studies using an RCT design, while the
1362	                                        previous evidence did not limit the study types for qualitative and quantitative syntheses.
1363	                                        Although, in our narrative analysis, most studies supported a significant effect of MBI
1364	                                        on athletes’ mental health indicators, the meta-analysis results did not yield a significant
1365	                                        effect size. Considering the limited number of studies in the analysis as well as the high
1366	                                        heterogeneity, we are not able to provide convincing evidence on the MBI intervention
1367	                                        effects on improving the mental health outcomes among athletes, which to some extent
1368	                                        emphasize the importance and requirements of more high quality RCTs on this domain.
1369	                                              Several limitations of this review should be noted. First, despite our efforts to imple-
1370	                                        ment a thorough literature search in the limited databases, we might omit some studies
1371	                                        due to the settings of search strategies (e.g., only limited to English language). Moreover,
1372	                                        due to the limited number of studies, we were not able to conduct a subgroup analysis to
1373	                                        further identify the moderators (e.g., participants characteristics, MBI types, and outcome
1374	                                        measures) that could explain the high degree of heterogeneity. The small number of studies
1375	                                        could also result in the cautious interpretation of the research findings. In addition, we did
1376	 Int. J. Environ. Res. Public Health 2023, 20, 2038                                                                                         13 of 16
1377	
1378	
1379	
1380	
1381	                                        not examine the potential mediators in the MBI programs due to the lack of relevant data
1382	                                        such that a further understanding of the underlying mechanisms could not be identified.
1383	                                              Despite these limitations, our research findings add values to future research and
1384	                                        interventions on MBIs among athletes. Our findings suggest that MBIs may be a potentially
1385	                                        effective approach for improving athletes’ sport performance; however, more strict empiri-
1386	                                        cal studies (e.g., RCT and cluster-RCT) should be undertaken to further identify the effec-
1387	                                        tiveness of MBIs and its dose–response effect with athletic performance. Furthermore, MBIs
1388	                                        had moderate-to-large effect sizes on enhancing athletes’ mindfulness and mindfulness-
1389	                                        related psychological components (e.g., flow, acceptance, and self-compassion), implying
1390	                                        that future studies could use MBIs to achieve specific training targets (e.g., enhancement of
1391	                                        emotional control and improvement of flow and commitment). In addition, our findings
1392	                                        could not provide convincing quantitative evidence for the effectiveness of MBIs on athletes’
1393	                                        mental health outcomes due to the limited number of included studies. More RCT studies
1394	                                        focusing on the mental health aspects among athletes are warranted in the future.
1395	
1396	                                        5. Conclusions
1397	                                             In conclusion, our systematic review and meta-analysis provided preliminary support
1398	                                        for the effectiveness of MBIs in promoting athletic performance, mindfulness level, and
1399	                                        mindfulness-related psychological components among athletes. The research findings also
1400	                                        suggest that more high-quality studies using a rigorous empirical design (e.g., RCT) are
1401	                                        warranted in the future, especially with respect to the mental health domains of athletes.
