                                        4. Discussion
                                              This is the first study that systematically reviewed and meta-analyzed the RCT ev-
                                        idence regarding the effectiveness of MBIs on athletic performance, mindfulness levels,
                                        mindfulness-related psychological components, and mental health outcomes among ath-
                                        letes. Thirty-two eligible studies were included in the narrative synthesis, of which nineteen
                                        were included in the quantitative analysis. Narratively, the MBIs were effective in promot-
                                        ing athletes’ sports performance. The results of the meta-analysis found that MBIs showed
                                        effectiveness on improving the mindfulness and mindfulness-based psychological compo-
                                        nents, yet no significant effects were found for mental health outcomes among athletes.
                                              For athletic performance, from the narrative synthesis, we found that all the included
                                        studies indicated a significant improvement in the performance indicators after receiving
                                        the MBI. Our finding is consistent with the previous review papers supporting for the
                                        effectiveness of MBIs on athletes’ sport performance [9,12]. However, due to the limited
                                        evidence and considerable variety in the outcome measures, a quantitative synthesis is
                                        not available. More studies using an RCT design to examine the effects of using MBIs in
                                        athletes’ sports performance are needed in the future.
                                              For mindfulness levels, in accordance with previous evidence [59,60], our study found
                                        that MBIs could significantly improve the athletes’ mindfulness levels. For the mindfulness-
                                        related psychological components (e.g., acceptance, flow, psychological flexibility, and
                                        ruminative response), we found a significant effect of MBIs on improving these indicators,
                                        which is in line with previous evidence among different types of athletes and general
                                        populations [10,61,62]. During the games, it is easy for athletes to experience negative
                                        emotions, such as nervousness and worries [63,64]. On game day, players may experience
                                        dissatisfaction with their performance, negative thinking, reality avoidance, and immersion
                                        in unpleasant emotions due to off-court circumstances, such as the unfavorable response
                                        of the crowd or losing points [65,66]. Mindfulness may play a crucial role in addressing
                                        these problems for athletes. Our research findings preliminarily supported the effects of
                                        MBIs on improving these mindfulness-related psychological components, implying that,
                                        in future practice, MBI could be applied in relevant sports domains to achieve specific
                                        training targets (e.g., enhancement of emotion control, prevention of performance failure
                                        under pressure, and improvement of flow and commitment).
                                              For the mental health outcomes, our findings were inconsistent with the previous evi-
                                        dence that showed that MBIs were effective in improving mental health symptoms [19,62].
                                        The potential reasons for the discrepancy may be multifaceted. For example, our review
                                        targeted all types of athletes, while previous studies focused on the elite athletes or general
                                        populations. Another reason MBIs may have not demonstrated improvements in mental
                                        health symptoms of athletes is because the athletes in the studies that were selected for
                                        our review are not clinical populations. It may have been that athletes’ mental health
                                        symptoms were already low; therefore, changes in mental health outcomes may have been
                                        inconsequential. In addition, we only included studies using an RCT design, while the
                                        previous evidence did not limit the study types for qualitative and quantitative syntheses.
                                        Although, in our narrative analysis, most studies supported a significant effect of MBI
                                        on athletes’ mental health indicators, the meta-analysis results did not yield a significant
                                        effect size. Considering the limited number of studies in the analysis as well as the high
                                        heterogeneity, we are not able to provide convincing evidence on the MBI intervention
                                        effects on improving the mental health outcomes among athletes, which to some extent
                                        emphasize the importance and requirements of more high quality RCTs on this domain.
                                              Several limitations of this review should be noted. First, despite our efforts to imple-
                                        ment a thorough literature search in the limited databases, we might omit some studies
                                        due to the settings of search strategies (e.g., only limited to English language). Moreover,
                                        due to the limited number of studies, we were not able to conduct a subgroup analysis to
                                        further identify the moderators (e.g., participants characteristics, MBI types, and outcome
                                        measures) that could explain the high degree of heterogeneity. The small number of studies
                                        could also result in the cautious interpretation of the research findings. In addition, we did
 Int. J. Environ. Res. Public Health 2023, 20, 2038                                                                                         13 of 16




                                        not examine the potential mediators in the MBI programs due to the lack of relevant data
                                        such that a further understanding of the underlying mechanisms could not be identified.
                                              Despite these limitations, our research findings add values to future research and
                                        interventions on MBIs among athletes. Our findings suggest that MBIs may be a potentially
                                        effective approach for improving athletes’ sport performance; however, more strict empiri-
                                        cal studies (e.g., RCT and cluster-RCT) should be undertaken to further identify the effec-
                                        tiveness of MBIs and its dose–response effect with athletic performance. Furthermore, MBIs
                                        had moderate-to-large effect sizes on enhancing athletes’ mindfulness and mindfulness-
                                        related psychological components (e.g., flow, acceptance, and self-compassion), implying
                                        that future studies could use MBIs to achieve specific training targets (e.g., enhancement of
                                        emotional control and improvement of flow and commitment). In addition, our findings
                                        could not provide convincing quantitative evidence for the effectiveness of MBIs on athletes’
                                        mental health outcomes due to the limited number of included studies. More RCT studies
                                        focusing on the mental health aspects among athletes are warranted in the future.

                                        5. Conclusions
                                             In conclusion, our systematic review and meta-analysis provided preliminary support
                                        for the effectiveness of MBIs in promoting athletic performance, mindfulness level, and
                                        mindfulness-related psychological components among athletes. The research findings also
                                        suggest that more high-quality studies using a rigorous empirical design (e.g., RCT) are
                                        warranted in the future, especially with respect to the mental health domains of athletes.

{
 "id": "Q78",
 "sourceFile": "Workload efficiency as a new tool to describe external and internal competitive match load of a professional soccer team A descriptive study on the.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Workload efficiency as a new tool to describe external and internal competitive match load of a professional soccer team: A descriptive study on the relationship between pre-game training loads and relative match load' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains": ["Monitoring & Technology", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Soccer"],
 "populations": ["Male Athletes", "Healthy Athletes", "Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Observational study of 14 healthy male players from one Austrian Second League professional team over a 13-week season, with 44 training sessions and 16 competitive matches tracked by 10 Hz GPS and heart-rate sensors. The authors define a new 'workload efficiency' index (equivalent distance divided by TRIMPMOD) and used hierarchical regression on training loads from D-1 to D-5. Sprint distance at D-3 and D-4 and total distance at D-1 were positive predictors of match workload efficiency, while Polar training load and training duration at D-1 were negative predictors; together the five variables explained 26.6 percent of variance.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Only 14 players from one team were studied, and the model is a team-average model in observational data. Heart-rate-based internal load can be affected by stress, hydration and caffeine, and the authors state that the index still needs validation and that they cannot say manipulating training would improve match performance.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat the timing advice (sprint work 3 to 4 days out, avoid long or hard sessions the day before) as a proven pre-match prescription, when the study is observational, explains only 26.6 percent of variance, and did not test whether changing training improves matches.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2019,
  "citation": "Grünbichler J, Federolf P, Gatterer H. Workload efficiency as a new tool to describe external and internal competitive match load of a professional soccer team: A descriptive study on the relationship between pre-game training loads and relative match load. Eur J Sport Sci. 2019.",
  "doi": "10.1080/17461391.2019.1697374",
  "abstract": "Training and match data from one professional team (14 players, 44 training sessions, 16 matches) were used to build a workload efficiency index and test whether loads in the five days before a match predicted it.",
  "tldr": "In one second-division team, higher sprint distance 3 to 4 days before a match and higher total distance the day before were linked to better match workload efficiency, while high load and long sessions the day before were linked to worse efficiency. The evidence is observational and needs testing before it changes pre-match planning.",
  "methods": "Observational study using Polar Team Pro 10 Hz GPS and heart-rate sensors. For each match, workload efficiency was equivalent distance divided by TRIMPMOD. Z-scored training variables from D-1 to D-5 were entered into a hierarchical multiple regression as predictors.",
  "findings": "Positive predictors of match workload efficiency: sprint distance at D-3 (beta 0.477), total distance at D-1 (beta 0.380) and sprint distance at D-4 (beta 0.312). Negative predictors: Polar training load at D-1 (beta -0.259) and training duration at D-1 (beta -0.216). The model explained 26.6 percent of variance (corrected R2 0.266).",
  "limitations": "Small sample from a single team, with a team-average model that the authors say may not hold for individuals. Heart-rate and GPS-based measures are affected by factors such as psychological stress, temperature and GPS validity at high speeds and accelerations. The design is observational and does not support causal advice.",
  "practicalImplications": "Consider scheduling the main sprint work 3 to 4 days before matches and keeping the day before short and low in load, matching this team's pattern. Treat the efficiency index as a monitoring idea to test in your own squad rather than as a target.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: The index may help staff compare how efficiently players turn pre-match training into match output, but with 26.6 percent of variance explained it should sit alongside other monitoring data. The sprint-timing and pre-match load patterns are candidates for a controlled trial.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The study does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to play, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q79",
 "sourceFile": "Workload monotony strain and non-contact injury incidence in professional football players.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Workload monotony, strain and non-contact injury incidence in professional football players' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance", "Sports Medicine & Injury", "Monitoring & Technology"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Sports Medicine", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Soccer"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Season-long cohort (2014 to 2015) of 130 professional players from five clubs in top European leagues, all playing UEFA competitions. Internal load was measured with session-RPE, and 237 non-contact injuries occurred over 30,887 days of observation (7.4 per 1000 h). Poisson regression found that higher 4-week monotony was associated with lower injury incidence (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.90) and higher 4-week strain with higher incidence (RR 1.50, 95% CI 1.14 to 1.97); the 1-, 2- and 3-week measures showed no significant link.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The design is observational, so the associations do not show that monotony or strain cause injury. Only five teams were studied, and the authors note that staff who saw the workload data may have adjusted sessions. The monotony finding runs opposite to an earlier youth-academy study, and prediction accuracy was not tested.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the 4-week monotony result as a rule that more regular workloads protect players, when it is a population-level association from one season of five teams that reverses an earlier finding and was not tested for predictive accuracy.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2018,
  "citation": "Delecroix B, Mccall A, Dawson B, Berthoin S, Dupont G. Workload monotony, strain and non-contact injury incidence in professional football players. Science and Medicine in Football. 2018.",
  "doi": "10.1080/24733938.2018.1508881",
  "abstract": "Season-long cohort of 130 elite players from five European teams, with internal workload from session-RPE. Poisson regression tested weekly, 2-week, 3-week and 4-week monotony and strain against non-contact injury incidence.",
  "tldr": "In five European professional squads, a high 4-week workload strain was associated with more non-contact injuries and a high 4-week monotony with fewer. These are associations from one observational season, so use them alongside other factors rather than as injury thresholds.",
  "methods": "Internal load was session-RPE multiplied by session or match duration for all training and matches. Monotony (mean divided by standard deviation) and strain (monotony multiplied by load) were calculated daily over rolling 1 to 4 week windows and related to injury incidence with Poisson regression.",
  "findings": "237 non-contact injuries, 7.4 per 1000 h, of which 58 were re-injuries that were counted in the total. 4-week monotony: RR 0.72 (95% CI 0.58 to 0.90; P = 0.004). 4-week strain: RR 1.50 (95% CI 1.14 to 1.97; P = 0.004). Monotony and strain over 1 to 3 weeks were not significantly associated with incidence.",
  "limitations": "The authors state that the association does not establish causation and that staff who recorded the workload may have adapted sessions. session-RPE is subjective, and re-injuries are included in the 237 injuries analysed. The predictive value of the measures was not assessed.",
  "practicalImplications": "Track 4-week strain (load multiplied by monotony) alongside other measures, and watch for sustained very high, very regular load across congested fixture periods. Also reduce large day-to-day swings between rest, training and match days, as the authors suggest. Do not use either measure as a stand-alone injury threshold.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Sustained high strain across a month of congested fixtures is worth monitoring, since it was linked to more injuries that would cut into training time. The study does not measure performance outcomes.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The study covers injury incidence across squads, not return to play, so it cannot inform when an injured player is ready to come back."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q81",
 "sourceFile": "Zurich to Berlin - ''Where'' Are We Now with the Concussion in Sport Group_.pdf",
 "decision": "DEGRADED",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "The article's own DOI is not printed in the extracted text. The only DOI in the text is the reference-list DOI for the fifth consensus statement (10.1136/bjsports-2017-097699), which does not count. The operator may verify the DOI externally and upgrade the decision.",
 "doiMissing": true,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Zurich to Berlin: Where Are We Now with the Concussion in Sport Group?' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Brain Health & Psychology", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Rehabilitation"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Injured Athletes", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative critique of the fifth Concussion in Sport Group consensus statement (Berlin 2016), going through its 11 Rs framework and the changes from the fourth statement, with reference to the systematic reviews that supported it. The authors report that the statement leaves most management to clinical judgement, that several recommendations (for example baseline neuropsychological testing and rest guidance) have weak support, and that many questions, including recovery prediction and the 24-hour step interval, remain open. No sample is studied.",
 "screeningLimitations": "No search method is described for this commentary, so it is a critical narrative rather than a systematic review, and the choice of points reflects the authors' own view. Because the article's DOI is not in the text, the record cannot be confirmed as the published version without external checking.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could take this paper as a summary of the consensus position, when it is a critical reading that questions several of the statement's recommendations, such as routine baseline testing and the step timing, on the authors' interpretation of the evidence.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2018,
  "citation": "Pusateri ME, Hockenberry BJ, McGrew CA. Zurich to Berlin: 'Where' Are We Now with the Concussion in Sport Group? Curr Sports Med Rep. 2018;17(1):26-30.",
  "doi": "",
  "abstract": "A review of the fifth Concussion in Sport Group consensus statement (Berlin 2016), covering the 11 Rs and the main changes to sideline evaluation, return to play and return to learn.",
  "tldr": "A critical review of the fifth Concussion in Sport Group statement that argues many of its recommendations lack evidence and that much management is still clinical judgement. Useful for seeing the limits of current consensus, not as a stand-alone protocol.",
  "methods": "Section-by-section narrative review and critique of the fifth consensus statement, referring to the 12 systematic reviews that supported it. No search strategy for the commentary is described.",
  "findings": "The statement adds a rehabilitation section and a return-to-learn outline, moves away from complete rest after the first 24 to 48 hours, and states that baseline testing is not mandatory. It does not support impact sensors for clinical diagnosis. The authors note that the 24-hour minimum per return-to-play step has little direct evidence, and that more than 90 percent of repeat concussions occur within 10 days of the last one.",
  "limitations": "This is a critical commentary, not a systematic review, and it does not show how often its critiques apply in practice. The DOI is not printed in the text.",
  "practicalImplications": "Use the SCAT5, same-day removal from play, serial monitoring and the stepwise return-to-sport framework as the consensus baseline, while noting the authors' point that the step intervals and baseline testing are weakly supported. For school-age athletes, prioritise return to learn before return to sport.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: The paper gives no guidance on performance training. Its one point relevant to performance staff is that baseline testing is not needed to interpret post-injury SCAT scores.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The consensus progression runs from symptom-limited activity through to full contact in steps of at least 24 hours, with no return on the day of injury. The authors say the step intervals have little direct evidence, and that the 10-day window after a concussion is the main period of repeat risk, so it can inform timing but not individual readiness decisions."
 }
}

 "decision": "INCLUDE",

 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "The filename is an 8.3 stub ('_EFFECT~2.PDF') so the full title cannot be compared; its leading word matches the text title 'Effects of Mindfulness-Based Interventions on Promoting Athletic Performance and Related Factors among Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trial'. Accepted as the named article on that basis.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Brain Health & Psychology",
 "domains": ["Brain Health & Psychology", "Training & Performance", "Athlete Wellbeing"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Male Athletes", "Female Athletes", "Professional / Elite", "Collegiate", "Youth / Adolescent", "Adult / Recreational", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review of 32 randomised controlled trials of mindfulness-based interventions in athletes (1,788 athletes in total, mean age 23.7 years, across many sports and levels), searched in five databases with no date limit. Seven trials were reported in the abstract as meta-analysed, but the results report pooled analyses of 3 trials (mindfulness; SMD 0.50, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.83), 5 trials (mindfulness-related psychological components; SMD 0.81, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.10) and 4 trials (mental health; SMD -0.03, 95% CI -0.35 to 0.29, not significant). Performance was synthesised narratively, with the authors reporting that all included studies showed improvement.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Each pooled analysis rests on only 3 to 5 trials, with high heterogeneity (I2 up to 89 percent), so the estimates are fragile. The paper's own study counts conflict (seven in the abstract, twelve across the results, nineteen in the discussion), and 6 of 32 trials were rated high risk of bias.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the pooled effects as evidence that mindfulness training improves athletic performance, when performance was only summarised narratively across varied measures and the quantitative results are for mindfulness and psychological factors.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2023,
  "citation": "Wang Y, Lei SM, Fan J. Effects of Mindfulness-Based Interventions on Promoting Athletic Performance and Related Factors among Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trial. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2023;20:2038.",
  "doi": "10.3390/ijerph20032038",
  "abstract": "Systematic review of 32 randomised trials of mindfulness-based interventions in athletes, with meta-analysis of mindfulness, mindfulness-related psychological components and mental health outcomes. Performance was summarised narratively.",
  "tldr": "Across 32 randomised trials in many sports, mindfulness-based training was linked to moderate gains in mindfulness and large gains in related psychological factors such as flow, acceptance and self-compassion, with performance gains reported narratively and no pooled effect on mental health. The evidence base is small and varied, so treat it as a promising option rather than a proven one.",
  "methods": "PRISMA-based search of five databases with no date limit, registered on PROSPERO (CRD42022299940). Two reviewers screened and extracted data independently. Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane tool, pooled SMDs were calculated with random-effects models in RevMan 5.4, and publication bias was checked with funnel plots and Egger tests.",
  "findings": "Narrative synthesis: the authors report that all included studies showed significant performance improvement. Meta-analysis: mindfulness SMD 0.50 (95% CI 0.17 to 0.83; 3 studies; I2 45%); mindfulness-related psychological components SMD 0.81 (95% CI 0.53 to 1.10; 5 studies; I2 77%); mental health SMD -0.03 (95% CI -0.35 to 0.29; 4 studies; I2 89%). Funnel plots and Egger tests showed no significant publication bias (all P > 0.1). A sensitivity analysis excluding high risk-of-bias studies was consistent with the main results.",
  "limitations": "Pooled analyses include only 3 to 5 trials each, with high heterogeneity, and no subgroup analysis was possible. Only English-language studies were searched. The study counts differ across the abstract (seven meta-analysed), results and discussion (nineteen quantitatively analysed), so the exact trial set is unclear.",
  "practicalImplications": "Mindfulness-based training is a reasonable option to consider for athletes who need help with flow, acceptance or self-compassion, with the programme matched to that target. Do not expect a benefit for mental health symptoms, since the pooled result was null. Test any programme against your own squad's outcome measures before relying on it.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: The strongest pooled effects are on mindfulness and performance-related psychological factors such as flow and acceptance, so mindfulness is most defensible as a mental-skills tool for competition preparation. The performance benefit itself rests on narrative synthesis of varied measures.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The review does not assess rehabilitation or return-to-sport outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions."
 }
}
